paras: The Sour Lake expulsion notices were written notices posted in Sour Lake, Texas, on Wednesday, September 16, 1903, ordering the town's Black residents to leave. Many Black residents fled with their belongings, but a local judge swore in extra deputies, white residents promised them protection, and the town was reported quiet within two days. Two papers later reported that the notices, which claimed to come from a white committee, had been posted by a practical joker.
Sour Lake was described in the coverage as "the new oil town of Texas." The reports name no dispute, crime or other incident that came before the notices.

On Wednesday, September 16, written notices appeared at "several conspicuous places" in Sour Lake "commanding the negroes to leave." According to a New Orleans dispatch, the notices purported to be signed by a white committee and ordered all Black residents to leave the town immediately. A dispatch from Sour Lake said the notices caused "great consternation" and that Black men and women could be seen "going in all directions, carrying all their possessions with them" for several hours before nightfall.

The same dispatch reported that hardware stores sold many pistols, shotguns and rifles, with "the better class of white people being the purchasers," though it did not say why they bought them. Black residents appealed to their white friends for protection, and the dispatch said their requests were granted.

Judge Peet swore in a large number of extra deputies to keep the peace and had the promise of law-abiding citizens to help suppress any violence. By September 18 a telegraph brief reported that Black residents had been "assured of protection and all is quiet there." The New York Sun reported that "an investigation disclosed that the notices were posted by a practical joker," but it named no one, and no arrest appears in the coverage. A Texas news column at the end of the month said the "better element" of white people had advised Black residents to disregard the warning and that there had been no further developments.

The Sour Lake dispatch ran in Texas papers under the headline "Ordered to Leave," in the Waxahachie Daily Light on September 17 and almost word for word in the Bryan Morning Eagle the next day. The San Antonio Daily Light gave the episode a single line among its "Telegraph Brevities," and the Shiner Gazette reported it on September 30 in its "All Over Texas" column, attributing the notices to "unknown parties."

Outside Texas, the New York Sun carried a New Orleans dispatch headlined "Exile Notice a Joke," which ended with the finding that a joker had posted the notices. The Atlanta Constitution made the episode the opening of an editorial, "The Two Ways," saying that before the hoax was discovered the town's white citizens, "almost without exception," had joined to keep Black residents from being "driven off or disturbed." The editorial set this against Waterloo, Iowa, where it said "the cry has gone up that the city must be 'white' and that the negroes must leave," and concluded that "the contrasting pictures speak for themselves."
No Black-press account of the episode appears in the coverage.

Accounts differ on who posted the notices: they claimed to come from a white committee, the Sun and the Atlanta Constitution said an investigation traced them to a practical joker, and the Shiner Gazette spoke only of "unknown parties." None of these reports names the author or describes the investigation, and the original Sour Lake dispatch does not raise the possibility of a hoax.

reader.title: Sour Lake expulsion notices
bases: Posted notices ordered all Black residents to leave Sour Lake and many did leave, though officials and white citizens moved to keep them and two papers reported the notices were a hoax (A1, A3, A5, A6).
A Sour Lake dispatch (A1), a New Orleans dispatch (A3) and a Texas news brief (A6) independently report the notices ordering Black residents to leave; they differ only on who posted them.

accounts.label: Sour Lake dispatch
accounts.gist: Notices commanding Black residents to leave caused 'great consternation'; whites bought firearms, many Black residents left with their belongings, and those who appealed to white friends were granted protection.

accounts.label: New Orleans dispatch
accounts.gist: The notices purported to come from a white committee; Judge Peet swore in deputies, and an investigation found the notices were posted by a practical joker.

accounts.label: Texas news brief
accounts.gist: Unknown parties posted the notices; the better element told Black residents to disregard them and nothing further happened.

accounts.label: Atlanta Constitution editorial
accounts.gist: The whole white population joined to keep Black residents from being driven out before the notices were found to be a joke, unlike Waterloo, Iowa, where the city wanted them gone.

framing.detail: Texas papers ran the 'Ordered to Leave' dispatch of 'great consternation' and a one-line note that negroes were 'assured of protection and all is quiet.'
The New York Sun headlined it 'Exile Notice a Joke', closing on the finding that a practical joker posted the notices.
The Atlanta Constitution's editorial 'The Two Ways' praised Sour Lake's white citizens for preventing the expulsion and set it against Waterloo, Iowa, as a sectional point.

versions.value: Notices purported to be signed by a white committee, but an investigation found a practical joker posted them

conflicts.note: The Sour Lake dispatch (A1) names no author; the joker finding comes from a New Orleans dispatch and the Atlanta editorial, which give no name or details of the investigation.
